newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO debates merits of enlargement candidates.
newsitem.headline: NATO debates merits of enlargement candidates.

text.p: NATO foreign ministers debated formally for the first time on Thursday which countries to invite to join the alliance next July -- the most radical change in Europe's security landscape since World War Two.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, charged with drawing up the list of former communist states, set aside several hours for a lunch-time discussion on the first day of a two-day meeting in the Portuguese resort town of Sintra.

Fresh from negotiating a landmark security pact with Russia to ease Moscow's opposition to NATO's eastwards expansion, Solana insisted that only ministers could attend the session from which he hopes a consensus will start to emerge.
"This is the first formal discussion on enlargement," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
Former communist Warsaw pact members Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic lead the field of 11 countries to become the first new members of the West's military alliance since Spain in 1982.

Slovenia, which fulfils many of the formal conditions, and Romania, backed strongly by France and Italy, have made strong late challenges, complicating the process of how to expand the alliance without weakening it.

NATO has said any former communist country wishing to be considered must have established democratic control of its armed forces, set up a market economy, and be attempting to make its forces compatible with those of the alliance.
But privately officials admit the decision on who to invite at a special summit in Madrid on July 8-9 is essentially political, and fraught with political danger.

NATO capitals, which see enlargement as a crucial element in an emerging European post-Cold War security order, are desperate to avoid creating new divisions between those gaining admittance and those that do not.

Underlining this, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and others have been at pains to insist the enlargement process will continue after Madrid, and have also agreed an enhanced partnership programme for other states.
Albright, who was expected to underscore the U.S. preference for three, would insist countries not chosen for membership this year must be given assurances that the door remains open, Burns said.
In remarks prepared for the meeting Albright was also quoted as saying new members must meet the highest possible standards before they join and be able to contribute to NATO's common security.
"First we want to make NATO stronger and more cohesive by adding new allies who are eager and able to contribute to our common security," Albright said.

"We want the first round of enlargement to be seen as a solid success in these terms and we want to be backed by strong parliamentary and public majorities," she said in her statement, made available by the State Department.
NATO officials stressed no decisions would be taken at the Sintra meeting, but said Solana was looking for sufficient guidance to find consensus on a number of countries by the end of June.
"He also wants to visit the capitals of aspiring members to inform them formally of the decision," said one official.
The ministers must also tackle the tricky issue of whether to invite the leaders of all applicant countries to Madrid or only the leaders of those set to be invited to join.

The three Baltic states, all of which are desperate to join but given little change of making it, are keen to attend the meeting to demonstrate their new independence and links with the West and underline their case for admittance at a later date.

The Sintra meeting comes two days after NATO agreed a new security relationship with Moscow, effectively winning its grudging approval to at least a limited alliance expansion by setting up a permanent NATO-Russia Council at NATO headquarters.
But Russia has since made clear it would still balk at former Soviet Republics, such as the Baltic states or Ukraine, joining the organisation which won the Cold War without a shot being fired.
In the margins of the meeting, the ministers also initialled a security pact with Ukraine giving that country a special status above that of partnership, but not going as far as the deal with Russia.
The meeting also reviewed an overhaul of alliance command structures to make it more flexible and allow it to carry out more varied missions, such as the current peace mission in Bosnia.
